name: D-aspartic acid (DAA)

card.summary: An amino acid sold as a testosterone booster; early work suggested a hormonal role, but trials in trained men found no increase and, at higher intake, a decrease.
card.note: Three randomized trials in resistance-trained men reported no testosterone increase; one reported lower testosterone at the higher intake tested.

quick.overview:
D-aspartic acid is the mirror-image (D-form) of the common amino acid aspartic acid, found naturally in the pituitary gland and testes. It is sold as a sports supplement marketed for raising testosterone.

A 2009 study reported that sodium D-aspartate increased luteinizing hormone and testosterone in humans and rats. Later randomized trials in resistance-trained men found no testosterone rise, and one found lower testosterone at 6 grams per day.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory work in rats proposes that D-aspartate acts in the pituitary to increase LH release and in testicular Leydig cells to raise testosterone synthesis, via cGMP and cAMP signaling. Human trials in trained men did not show this effect.
quick.risks: The trials report no major safety signals, but one reported lower total and free testosterone with 6 g/day, and another reported a 16 percent drop in estradiol. It is sold as a dietary supplement; long-term safety data are limited.

lead: D-aspartic acid (DAA) is the D-enantiomer of aspartic acid, one of the few D-amino acids found in mammals; it is concentrated in tissues including the pituitary gland and testes rather than being built into proteins [1][2]. It is sold as a dietary supplement, often in testosterone-support and pre-workout blends, and lifters take it with the aim of raising testosterone to support muscle growth, strength and recovery, and through that a fuller, leaner physique.

The appeal rests on a 2009 report that sodium D-aspartate raised luteinizing hormone (LH) and testosterone in humans and rats [2]. Randomized, placebo-controlled trials in resistance-trained men published between 2013 and 2017 reported no rise in testosterone, and one reported lower testosterone at the higher intake tested [3][4][5]. A 2024 systematic review of 27 proposed testosterone boosters, which included two DAA studies, concluded that most failed to raise total testosterone versus placebo [6]. A small 2025 trial in men with idiopathic infertility, using a combination of DAA, ubiquinol and zinc, reported higher testosterone and sperm motility after three months [7].

On the T Nation forum, DAA appears in supplement stacks, in discussions of post-cycle recovery and in threads from men with low testosterone results, where some members report using it and others question the research behind it [8][9][10].
infobox: Powder or capsule, alone or in blends

paras: The 2009 study reported that the pituitary and testes synthesize D-aspartate from L-aspartate and take it up efficiently. In rat pituitary tissue it increased LH release and synthesis via cGMP signaling, and in rat Leydig cells it increased testosterone synthesis and release via cAMP [3]. Aspartate-related compounds such as NMDA act on glutamate receptors in the nervous system; D-aspartate is also described as a neuromodulator [1].
The 2009 report combined a human component, in which sodium D-aspartate was associated with higher LH and testosterone, with rat experiments [2].

In a 2013 trial, resistance-trained men took 3 g of DAA or placebo for 28 days alongside heavy training; total and free testosterone, LH, GnRH and estradiol were unchanged, and strength and body composition changes did not differ between groups [3]. A 2015 trial randomized 24 trained men to placebo, 3 g or 6 g daily for 14 days: 3 g did not differ from placebo, while total testosterone was lower in the 6 g group and free testosterone was lower than placebo [4]. A 2017 randomized trial in 22 trained men over 12 weeks of supervised training at 6 g daily found no change in total or free testosterone, a 16 percent fall in estradiol, and similar training outcomes in both groups; its authors wrote that DAA was ineffective at changing testosterone [5].

The 2024 systematic review of testosterone boosters in athletes, healthy men, men with late-onset hypogonadism and infertile men covered 52 studies and reported that most of the 27 supplements examined, DAA among them, did not raise total testosterone versus placebo [6]. In a 2025 randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 75 men with idiopathic infertility, a daily combination of 2660 mg DAA, ubiquinol and zinc was associated with higher progressive sperm motility and total testosterone at three months; the product was a combination, so the contribution of DAA alone was not separated [7].

The trials above did not report serious adverse events, but did report changes in hormone levels: lower total and free testosterone with 6 g/day in one trial, and reduced estradiol in another [4]. No long-term safety studies are available.

DAA is sold in the US as a dietary supplement, typically as a powder or in capsule blends marketed to lifters. It appears in T Nation supplement logs, in threads asking whether it helps men with low testosterone readings, and in post-cycle recovery discussions [8][9][10]. One member of a 2010 thread summarized early animal work on D-form amino acids and wondered whether it applied to lifters [9]; in a 2019 thread a member advised another with low testosterone to take DAA and ashwagandha, describing both as clinically proven [10].

lore.intro: On T Nation, DAA is discussed as one of several over-the-counter testosterone supports, alongside zinc, magnesium and herbal extracts [8][9][10].

claims.believers: Members cite the 2009 human and rat report and describe taking it when testosterone looked low, with one 2019 poster calling it clinically proven to boost testosterone [10][2].
claims.experts: Randomized trials in resistance-trained men reported no increase, and one reported lower testosterone at 6 g per day; a 2024 systematic review reached a similar overall finding for most boosters [3][4][5][6].

claims.claim: DAA helps recovery after a cycle of anabolic compounds
claims.believers: Threads from 2008 and 2012 discuss adding DAA to post-cycle routines to help restore natural testosterone [8][11].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested DAA in men recovering from anabolic steroid or prohormone use.

claims.claim: DAA supports fertility and sperm quality
claims.believers: Some users and supplement makers point to its presence in testes and to small studies in infertile men.
claims.experts: A 2025 randomized trial of a DAA, ubiquinol and zinc combination in infertile men reported higher motility and testosterone; it was a single combination study [7].

angle.text: Lifters take DAA hoping a higher testosterone level will translate into more muscle, strength and recovery, and so a more developed physique. Trials in trained men have measured hormones, strength and muscle size directly.
